File Hash Calculator

브라우저 내부 처리

Calculate SHA hashes for uploaded files locally in the browser.

File hash verification workflow

Comparing hashes is the reliable way to confirm a build artefact or received file was not corrupted in transit. Check the value computed here against the published checksum. The whole file is read in the browser and never uploaded, which makes it usable for internal files too.

Compare checksums

Compare a local file hash with the SHA-256 value published in release notes or download pages.

No upload required

The browser reads the file and computes the hash locally; the selected file is not uploaded by this tool.

Record multiple hashes

When needed, keep SHA-256 and SHA-512 values together in verification notes.

Errors you will hit

Case differences look like a mismatch

Hex digests are case insensitive. 9B2E and 9b2e are the same value — normalize the case before comparing.

The browser stalls on large files

Hashing happens in memory, so multi-gigabyte files can overwhelm the tab. Use an OS command such as shasum or certutil for those.

Can you trust a SHA-1 result?

SHA-1 has demonstrated collision attacks and is unsuitable for security verification. Use SHA-256 or stronger.

Things to check

Hashing is not encryption

A hash identifies file content and helps with integrity checks. It does not restore the original file or provide secrecy.

Large files take time

Very large files can use more browser memory and processing time. Wait briefly before assuming the calculation failed.

Different hashes mean different files, not the reverse

Matching hashes effectively mean identical files, but a slightly corrupted download produces a completely different hash. So a hash cannot tell you how much changed — that is a diff tool's job.

Large files take time

The hash is computed in your browser, so the whole file must be read. Multi-gigabyte files can be slow or hit memory limits. In exchange nothing is uploaded, which is what makes it safe for internal files.

SHA-1 is for integrity only now

Collisions in SHA-1 can be constructed deliberately, so it is unsuitable for signatures or security verification. It is still fine for checking whether a transfer corrupted a file. Use SHA-256 or stronger where security matters.

More: step-by-step usage and worked examples

How to use it

  1. Select the file you want to verify.
  2. Compare the calculated SHA value with the reference value from a release note, download page, or internal document.
  3. Ignore casing and extra whitespace when comparing hexadecimal strings.
  4. If the value differs, download the file again or review the transfer path.

Real input and output

Verifying a download

Input

ubuntu-24.04.iso

Output

SHA-256
9b2e1f...c47a3d

If a single character differs from the published checksum, the file is corrupted or tampered with.
